video_title: Linear vs. Exponential: AGI Has Arrived But Oil, Bonds and the Fed Oh My
gist: Jordi Visser argues investors are wasting attention on a 'linear' macro tape (oil, bond yields, Fed odds) while the week's real news is Jensen Huang declaring that AGI has arrived with the Astra model, which used 10,000 agents in parallel for 88 hours to hit the Navier-Stokes challenge. He builds the case that AI capex is rate-insensitive, that H100 rental prices being flat over three years and up 22% on the month destroys the GPU-depreciation bear case and could remove hundreds of billions in hyperscaler credit needs, that shortening corporate duration makes multiple compression the dominant equity risk, and that Robin Hood and Ethereum are the entry points to the TradFi/AI/crypto convergence.

insights.claim: Visser dates the break between the 'linear' economy driven by oil, bonds and rates and the 'exponential' economy to 2008, attributing it to the iPhone's release the year before plus growing transfer payments and government debt, and says the MAG 7 was the trade that expressed it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames any macro-first allocation process as structurally mispositioned; the implied tilt is toward exponential/tech exposure regardless of the rate cycle.
insights.quote: That all changed beginning in 2008. That is when the exponential world took off because of the release of iPhone the year before and because transfer payments started to grow

insights.claim: AI capex, not housing and autos, is the marginal driver of the US economy, and Visser argues it is not rate-sensitive at all — which is why rate-based economic forecasting now fails.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If the growth engine does not respond to the funds rate, Fed-path trades and rate-sensitive cyclicals lose their historical beta to the cycle.
insights.quote: AI capex is driving the economy. And as I showed last week, it is not at all rate sensitive.

insights.claim: Visser cites a week with hotter-than-expected core inflation and PPI, rising Fed odds, a crude rally and a worsening war, during which the S&P was still up slightly over two days, as a live falsification of macro-driven equity positioning.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: When bad macro prints produce no equity damage, the tape is confirming the driver has changed — a reason to stop trading the macro calendar.
insights.quote: the probability the Fed went up, crude oil went through, the war is getting worse, and over the two days, as of when I started doing this, the S&P was up slightly

insights.claim: Visser argues GDP is the wrong instrument for measuring the current productivity boom because it is a 1930s industrial-production index that does not count IP, so accelerating productivity shows up in profit margins rather than official statistics.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues for watching corporate margin series rather than official productivity prints to time the AI trade, and for reading lab-affiliated economists over sell-side rate forecasters.
insights.quote: The model of GDP is wrong. You can't say that GDP, the index created in the 1930s to measure industrial production, is the right metric to be using to say productivity is not higher.

themes.theme: Credit Tape and Policy Pressure on the Long End

insights.claim: Visser uses HYG relative to IEF as his real-time equity-risk overlay instead of quoted credit spreads, and notes HYG rose relative to IEF this week — high yield held in while Treasuries sold off — confirming the equity rally.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A liquid, intraday credit proxy that flagged the 2022 drawdown; a rollover in HYG/IEF would be the first sign the AI bid is breaking.
insights.quote: HYG relative to IEF, the proxy that I'll use real time and the one that I care the most about as an overlay rel instead of spreads.

insights.claim: Bond volatility, junk spreads and TIPS-implied inflation expectations all failed to move despite hot inflation prints and rising Fed odds, which Visser reads as cross-asset confirmation that the macro headlines are noise.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete condition for changing the view: fade macro-driven de-risking until credit or vol actually breaks.
insights.quote: bond va's not moving, junk spreads aren't moving. Uh any part the inflation expectations via tips not moving like the market is saying h we don't really care about what's going on.

insights.claim: Visser says the S&P's PEG ratio is the cheapest in at least 30 years, and rebuts the 'peak earnings' objection by pointing to earnings revisions still rising and profit margins — which historically roll over first — not yet turning down.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes an optically expensive index as cheap on growth-adjusted terms and identifies margin rollover, not the Fed, as the sell trigger to monitor.
insights.quote: the market has never been cheaper or at least in the last 30 plus years with the PEG ratio down here

insights.claim: Visser reports Bessent's upsized Treasury buybacks (to six billion) being immediately sold and floats that the fallback plan is to cut long-term issuance outright, framing the administration's fight with the bond market as one investors should not take the other side of.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An explicit policy path for suppressing the long end via supply rather than demand; Visser's conclusion is to avoid the fight rather than buy bonds.
insights.quote: Is it talk time to talk about plan B? If this doesn't work, they'll just cut long-term issuance outright.

themes.theme: AGI Arrival: Astra and Agent Swarms

insights.claim: Jensen Huang declared that AGI has arrived with the Astra model, which Visser says should have been the week's dominant news story rather than a 10 basis point move in bond yields.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If a credible capability threshold has been crossed, positioning against the AI complex is fighting a step-change rather than a cycle.
insights.quote: Jensen Yuang, the godfather of AI, said AGI has arrived with Astra.

insights.claim: Astra was trained on roughly 100,000 GPUs, the next model is four times that size, and the Vera Rubin generation sits behind it — a visible multi-generation compute escalation Visser uses to argue against fading the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A disclosed compute pipeline underwrites the capex forecasts that AI-infrastructure equities are discounting.
insights.quote: 100,000k is what basically Astro was trained on. The next model is four times the size and behind that the Vera Rubins. Why fade this guys?

insights.claim: Research agents are reportedly generating 3.1 workdays of output per human workday, and 10,000 AI agents running in parallel for 88 hours hit the Navier-Stokes challenge — which Visser argues has downstream implications for turbines, aircraft, cooling, reactors, batteries and medicine.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A quantified productivity multiple for digital labor plus a mechanism by which AI expands the total economic pie, not just corporate margins.
insights.quote: research agents are now generating 3.1 workdays for every human workday

insights.claim: Visser replaces the classic growth formula of more people plus more capital plus higher productivity with one where digital labor substitutes for population growth, so the binding constraint on GDP shifts from human headcount to compute, energy and deployment capacity.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reorients long-horizon growth exposure toward compute and power supply chains and away from demographic-driven growth assumptions.
insights.quote: The old constraint on GDP was ultimately the number of humans and the productivity of their time. The new constraint may increasingly become compute, energy, and our ability to deploy intelligence.

insights.claim: Demand for Astra is outrunning capacity — Visser cites 6.2 million views and says they are already running out of space — alongside Microsoft's plan to triple its data center computing power and its reiterated capacity shortage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Capacity shortage at the largest hyperscaler is the cleanest confirmation that the capex cycle has not peaked.
insights.quote: Demand for Astra is really unprecedented. 6.2 million views. They're running out of space for it already.

insights.claim: H100 rental prices are roughly unchanged from three years ago and rose 22% over the past month, versus a normal aging path Visser says would imply a 40-50% decline — directly falsifying the depreciation bear case associated with Michael Burry and Jim Chanos.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The most checkable datapoint in the AI-accounting debate; a sustained rollover in rental rates would revive the short thesis, continued strength invalidates it.
insights.quote: H100 rental prices are almost at the same level as they were three years ago. Think about that, guys. They're at the same price.

insights.claim: Visser points to Gavin Baker's call from a month earlier that the market wrongly assumed GPU rental prices would steadily fall, when older GPUs are in fact holding value and in some cases repricing higher — a call the subsequent month confirmed.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A named, dated call already validated by the tape, useful as a leading indicator for hyperscaler cash-flow revisions.
insights.quote: Instead, older GPUs were holding their value far better than expected. In some cases, rental prices were actually rising.

insights.claim: Because hyperscalers can reprice existing compute upward when contracts roll — Visser's analogy is buying tomatoes at $2 and selling at $20 — cloud cash-flow estimates are far too low and the sector may need hundreds of billions of dollars less credit than expected.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Second-order trade: if AI-related debt issuance shrinks rather than balloons, the AI-credit-bubble short and the associated spread widening both fail.
insights.quote: This could remove hundreds of billions of dollars of expected credit needs.

insights.claim: Visser's framing of the whole debate is that accounting depreciation schedules and the actual GPU rental market now disagree, and only one of them has real transactions behind it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Converts a narrative argument about AI accounting into a falsifiable test both bulls and bears can track.
insights.quote: whether or not you agree with it, the market is depreciating GPUs, the rental market is not, that's the issue

themes.theme: Terminal Value Compression and the Entrepreneurship Hedge

insights.claim: Visser's core valuation framework is that AI expands the total addressable economy through scientific breakthroughs while simultaneously shortening corporate duration, so the market's TAM grows even as individual companies' terminal values and multiples compress.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Explains how an index can be cheap on PEG while individual multiples de-rate — own the TAM-expansion beneficiaries, not incumbents priced on long-duration earnings.
insights.quote: we get to a point where the TAM gets bigger at the same time that corporate duration gets shorter

insights.claim: Visser says multiple compression already ran through software and is now hitting hardware, citing Nvidia trading at what he calls a cheap PE, and frames the unanswered question as what multiple a disrupted, no-longer-growing company deserves.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Warns that optically cheap PEs in AI hardware are the market pricing shortened duration rather than a valuation opportunity — screen on growth persistence.
insights.quote: Multiples are going to compress because terminal value, the ability to know when a company will have a cliff of their earnings no longer growing.

insights.claim: Visser caps expectations for AI hardware winners: he does not expect Micron to repeat its prior twelve-bagger, sees roughly 1,600 to 2,000 as realistic from about 1,000, and expects most days to be flat or down with roughly 5% of days carrying the entire annual return.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues against buy-and-hold in the AI leaders and for an entry-timing overlay, since missing about five days means missing the whole move.
insights.quote: at the end of the year, maybe 5% of the rally, the days will be the rallies you need to miss. And if you miss those five days, you miss the whole move.

insights.claim: Visser argues most coming layoffs will not come from thriving AI-enabled firms but from companies under competitive pressure because AI can now do what they do, and cites Sundar Pichai's warning that those who do not learn to orchestrate agents now will spend 2027 catching up.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Distinguishes 'AI efficiency' layoffs from 'AI disruption' layoffs and puts a 12-18 month clock on agent-orchestration skill as differentiating human capital.
insights.quote: They need to fire people because they're under pressure. And they're under pressure because AI can do these things all the time.

insights.claim: Visser's design principle for an AI trading desk is aggressive rejection — thousands of ideas daily, roughly 99% rejected at the first filter and 90% of survivors rejected at the next — explicitly mirroring how a multi-strategy allocator like Millennium screens managers.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes AI's quant edge as search-and-filter capacity rather than prediction; the value sits in the rejection rate, not the idea generation.
insights.quote: The great thing about a back test is it should fail most of the time. And to build an AI trading desk, the system is designed to reject almost everything.

insights.claim: Visser built a signal system for his 100-name AI universe around a structural-trend, reset, coiled, ignition sequence using average true range and rate of change, based on his view that changing market structure makes investors late to moves and forces earlier exits.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A replicable entry/exit overlay for a structural bull market where buy-and-hold is punishing; he credits it with exiting Micron well before the top.
insights.quote: I'm looking for structural bull markets. When things get overdone, I want to basically be out based on rate of change and then I want to wait for them to reset.

insights.claim: Over 80% of the 100 names in Visser's AI capex universe are above an upward-sloping 200-day moving average, which he treats as evidence of a structural bull market in AI infrastructure rather than a narrow rally.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Breadth within the theme is the health check; a drop below this threshold would signal the capex trade narrowing to a handful of names.

insights.claim: Visser argues momentum becomes the dominant factor at exponential inflection points because what worked over the past ten years is less useful for responding today.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues for rotating into momentum and away from mean-reversion and value frameworks calibrated on the post-GFC regime.
insights.quote: That's why I think momentum becomes a dominant factor

insights.claim: Robin Hood, Mumu and Interactive Brokers have all shipped agentic investing — Mumu since April 23rd with paper trading, APIs and proprietary price data Visser says beats Yahoo Finance — making retail deployment of multiple uncorrelated agent strategies an infrastructure reality as of June 2026.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Brokerages now compete on agent APIs and data quality, a new differentiation axis that should drive engagement, order flow and account acquisition.

themes.theme: Robin Hood Convergence and Tokenization Catalysts

insights.claim: Visser calls Robin Hood the epicenter of the AI-crypto-macro nexus — a trading company under-monetizing crypto relative to its other businesses that is also an agentic company — and says it is the best single entry point for understanding the convergence from an earnings perspective.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A single listed vehicle expressing three converging themes, with the under-monetized crypto segment as the optionality.
insights.quote: Robin Hood is basically the epicenter of AI crypto macro nexus.

insights.claim: Robin Hood chain has been live only two months and is already generating a record 6 million in daily fees, with Bernstein seeing 31% upside as its fees top Solana's — what Visser summarizes as 'the chain is now earnings'.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Onchain fee revenue is becoming a reportable earnings line for a listed brokerage, a fast-compounding stream TradFi research has barely modeled.
insights.quote: The chain is now earnings.

insights.claim: Visser notes Arbitrum surged 7.87% on Robin Hood chain news while a Wall Street Journal search for Arbitrum returned no results, arguing the coverage gap between crypto-native and traditional financial media is itself a repeatable alpha source.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Price-moving onchain catalysts go uncovered by TradFi media, creating a tractable information edge for anyone reading crypto-native sources.
insights.quote: Arbitron Wall Street Journal did not match any news results. Shocking.

insights.claim: Visser argues getting into tokenization ahead of TradFi is the trade because institutions will be forced in to generate alpha, with the Clarity Act the catalyst — though he puts odds of passage this year below 20% even as Coinbase's Brian Armstrong and Patrick Witt say it is ready for a yes vote.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Asymmetric setup: low near-term odds but a large institutional-credibility unlock, letting you position ahead of pension and institutional flows.
insights.quote: The probabilities for this year of getting it through are still below 20%. But that doesn't mean they can't get a yes vote.

insights.claim: Visser stacks the week's institutional tokenization signals — NASDAQ investing 100 million in Kraken targeting a 2027 tokenized stock launch, US banks testing stablecoins, Visa's stablecoin card business exploding, and European banks planning a euro stablecoin on Ethereum — as evidence incumbents are already preparing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Institutional infrastructure is being built out ahead of the regulatory framework, which front-runs the flow rather than following it.

themes.theme: Valuing Ethereum and the AI Trust Premium

insights.claim: Visser believes Ethereum should outperform Bitcoin in a genuine bull market because of its ecosystem and network effects on the agentic side, and notes Ethereum broke out against Bitcoin to its highest level since January.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A specific relative-value expression tied to the agentic thesis rather than to generic crypto beta.
insights.quote: I think Ethereum should be outperforming Bitcoin when we're actually in the bull market

insights.claim: Visser grades William Mougayar's decade-old TED talk on Ethereum as 8/10 on direction but 5/10 on specifics: too aggressive on removing intermediaries, blind to stablecoins, and above all missing AI agents — which Visser says may be what finally makes the original disintermediation thesis work.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The thesis failed because it assumed human users; agent-to-agent transaction demand is the missing driver that would revalue the base layer.
insights.quote: The biggest thing he didn't see was AI agents and this ironically they may finally make his thesis work.

insights.claim: Visser draws a direct analogy between Ethereum and Amazon: Amazon ran roughly 27,000% from its 1997 online-bookstore days to 2013 while never having a PE below 100 until 2017-2018, and Ethereum is up about 3,000% from its lows — implying most of the move happens before any accepted valuation framework exists.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An explicit warning to institutional allocators that waiting for a defensible valuation model is how you miss the move, as he says he personally did with Amazon.
insights.quote: when you're trying to figure out how to value crypto by the time it gets to the point where it's no longer a ridiculous price, you've already lost 27,000%

insights.claim: Visser argues AI turns trust into a priced economic asset and that Ethereum is the trust model, concluding that every real-world asset will have to move onchain for the blockchain to retain its value.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Positions real-world-asset tokenization as necessary rather than optional and frames Ethereum's moat as verification rather than throughput.
insights.quote: AI makes trust an economic asset. I'm 100% sure that the blockchain needs every real world asset to go on there to keep its value.

insights.claim: Visser links escalating AI-enabled cyberattacks — Iranian hackers shutting a UK power plant, Boston Scientific cutting its earnings forecast on cyberattack fallout alongside Stryker, and Anthropic disclosing a fourth AI hacking incident involving Opus 4.6 — to his crypto bullishness, arguing AI destroys trust in everything while disproportionately hurting small companies that cannot defend themselves.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Cyber risk is now an earnings-guidance event; the second-order read is that it accrues to verifiable-trust infrastructure and penalizes small-cap balance sheets.
insights.quote: I think AI leads to not trusting anything and it will not stop the earnings. It will not stock productivity, but it will hurt smaller businesses and smaller companies that can't protect themselves.
